questions.stem: What is the original source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
options: Light energy from the sun
Chemical energy in the soil
Heat energy from the Earth's core
Kinetic energy from wind
questions.explanation: Producers capture light energy from the sun in photosynthesis and store it as chemical energy in organic compounds, which then passes along food chains. A few deep-sea communities rely on chemical energy instead, but they are the exception.

questions.stem: What do decomposers such as fungi and bacteria do in an ecosystem?
options: Capture light energy and convert it into chemical energy
Feed only on living plants, which keeps all plant numbers in check
Hunt and eat herbivores at the top of the food web
Break down dead matter and wastes, returning nutrients to the soil
questions.explanation: Decomposers obtain energy by breaking down dead organisms and wastes, releasing inorganic nutrients that producers can reuse. Capturing light energy is the role of producers.

questions.stem: Why does energy flow through an ecosystem in one direction while matter cycles?
options: Energy is lost as heat at each level, but atoms are reused by producers
Energy is recycled by decomposers, but matter is lost as heat at each level
Energy and matter are both lost from the ecosystem at every trophic level
Energy is stored permanently in the soil, while matter returns to the sun
questions.explanation: At each transfer much of the energy is released as heat from respiration and cannot be reused by producers. Atoms such as carbon and nitrogen are returned to the environment by decomposers and taken up again.

questions.stem: In a food chain, producers store 50 000 kJ of energy. If about 10% passes to each next trophic level, how much reaches the secondary consumers?
options: 500 kJ
50 kJ
questions.explanation: About 10% of 50 000 kJ (5000 kJ) reaches the primary consumers, and 10% of that (500 kJ) reaches the secondary consumers. The figure 5000 kJ stops one level too early.

questions.stem: Why is only a small fraction of the energy in one trophic level passed on to the next?
options: Most is destroyed when organisms die, so it disappears from the whole ecosystem completely
Producers send most of their energy straight to the top predators in the food web
Consumers store all the energy they eat, but release it only when they die
Much is used in respiration and lost as heat, or stays in uneaten and undigested parts
questions.explanation: Organisms use most of the energy they take in for respiration, which releases heat, and parts of their food are not eaten or not digested. Energy is not destroyed; it leaves the food chain as heat.

questions.stem: In a food web, a fox eats rabbits, which eat grass, and also eats spiders, which eat grasshoppers that feed on grass. Which statement is correct?
options: The fox is a decomposer, because it feeds on animals that have eaten plant material
The fox is a secondary consumer when it eats rabbits and a tertiary consumer when it eats spiders
The fox is a primary consumer when it eats rabbits and a secondary consumer when it eats the spiders
The fox is a producer, because the energy it gains originally came from the grass
questions.explanation: Rabbits are primary consumers, so a fox eating them is a secondary consumer. Spiders eat grasshoppers (primary consumers), so spiders are secondary consumers and a fox eating them is a tertiary consumer; one animal can feed at more than one trophic level in a food web.

questions.stem: What does a biomass pyramid show?
options: The order in which species colonise a habitat
The mass of living material at each trophic level
The number of different species at each trophic level
The rate at which energy enters the food chain
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid represents the total dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time. Numbers of individuals are shown in a pyramid of numbers.

questions.stem: In some ocean ecosystems the biomass of phytoplankton at any moment is less than the biomass of the zooplankton that eat them. How is this possible?
options: Phytoplankton reproduce so quickly that a small standing biomass supports more consumers
Zooplankton make their own food by photosynthesis, so they need no phytoplankton
Energy increases at each trophic level in the ocean, unlike energy on land
Phytoplankton are not producers, so they do not form the base of the pyramid
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid is a snapshot, and fast-growing, fast-reproducing phytoplankton are eaten almost as quickly as they are produced. Over time they still supply more energy than the zooplankton receive, so an energy pyramid is never inverted.

questions.stem: Rabbits are removed from a food web in which they are eaten by foxes and eagles and compete with kangaroos for grass. What is the most likely short-term effect?
options: Fox and eagle numbers fall, while grass and kangaroo numbers rise
Fox and eagle numbers rise, while grass and kangaroo numbers fall
Only grass is affected, because rabbits feed on nothing else
Kangaroos fall, because they relied on rabbits for their food
questions.explanation: Predators lose a food source, and the competitor gains more of the shared grass. Food webs let you trace such effects through every link connected to the removed species.

questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, which process takes carbon dioxide out of the air?
options: Photosynthesis
Cellular respiration
Combustion
Decomposition
questions.explanation: Producers take in carbon dioxide and fix the carbon into organic compounds during photosynthesis. Respiration, combustion and decomposition all release carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How does carbon in the body of a dead banksia return to the atmosphere?
options: Decomposers respire as they break down the dead tissue, releasing CO2
Producers absorb it directly from the dead tissue through their leaves
It turns straight into nitrogen gas, which then escapes into the air
It stays in the soil permanently, because carbon cannot be recycled
questions.explanation: Decomposers use the organic compounds in dead matter for respiration, releasing carbon dioxide. Carbon is recycled; it does not change into nitrogen.

questions.stem: How does burning fossil fuels affect the carbon cycle?
options: It has no effect, because the carbon was already in the atmosphere
It releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years
It removes carbon from the atmosphere and stores it in new rock layers
It turns atmospheric carbon dioxide into methane in the oceans
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed from organisms buried long ago, so burning them adds carbon to the atmosphere faster than natural processes remove it. This raises atmospheric carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Besides producers, what is another major store that takes up carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
options: Rivers, where carbon dioxide is turned into nitrogen
The oceans, where carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater
The ozone layer, where carbon dioxide is broken down
Glaciers, where carbon dioxide freezes into blocks of solid ice
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolves in the oceans, which hold a large store of carbon, some of it used by marine organisms to build shells. The ozone layer does not take up carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: In a year, photosynthesis in a forest takes up 120 units of carbon, while respiration by its plants, animals and decomposers releases 100 units. What is the forest's net effect on atmospheric carbon?
options: It has no effect, because all of the carbon it takes up is respired
It is a carbon sink, storing all 120 units of the carbon it took up
It is a carbon sink, storing 20 units of carbon in that year
It is a carbon source, adding 20 units of carbon to the air
questions.explanation: The forest takes up 20 more units than it releases, so it removes carbon from the atmosphere and stores it as biomass and soil organic matter. Only the difference between uptake and release is stored, not the full 120 units.

questions.stem: Why can most plants and animals not use nitrogen gas directly from the air?
options: Nitrogen gas is far too rare in the air for any organism to obtain enough of it
Nitrogen gas is toxic, so organisms must keep it out of all their cells
Nitrogen gas dissolves only in seawater, out of reach of land organisms
The triple bond in N2 can be broken only by specialised organisms or lightning
questions.explanation: Atmospheric nitrogen makes up about 78% of air, but its strong triple bond means it must first be fixed by certain bacteria or by lightning. Plants then take up nitrogen as nitrate or ammonium ions.

questions.stem: What is nitrogen fixation?
options: Converting proteins in dead organisms into ammonium ions
Converting nitrites into nitrates in well-aerated soil
Converting nitrogen gas into ammonia or other usable compounds
Converting nitrates back into nitrogen gas in waterlogged soil
questions.explanation: Fixation turns unusable N2 into ammonia, which can be built into living things. Turning nitrates back into nitrogen gas is denitrification.

questions.stem: Legumes such as acacias have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria called rhizobia. How does this relationship benefit the plant?
options: The bacteria convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas
The bacteria produce oxygen, which the roots use in respiration
The bacteria fix nitrogen gas into compounds the plant can use
The bacteria take in carbon dioxide and pass it to the leaves
questions.explanation: The rhizobia fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, supplying the plant, while the plant provides the bacteria with sugars: a mutualism. This lets legumes grow in nitrogen-poor soils.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes nitrification?
options: Nitrate is converted to nitrite, then nitrite to nitrogen gas, by soil bacteria
Nitrogen gas is converted to ammonium by lightning, then taken up by plants
Proteins are converted to ammonium by decomposers, then lost to the air
Ammonium is converted to nitrite, then nitrite to nitrate, by soil bacteria
questions.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then nitrite to nitrate, the form most readily taken up by plants. Converting nitrate to nitrogen gas is denitrification.

questions.stem: A farmer notices that crops on a waterlogged paddock show nitrogen deficiency, even though fertiliser was applied. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Low oxygen favours denitrifying bacteria that turn nitrate into nitrogen gas
Low oxygen favours nitrifying bacteria, which make extra nitrate in the soil
Water fixes nitrogen gas into ammonia faster than the plants can absorb it
Waterlogging stops decomposers working, so nitrogen gas builds up in roots
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria thrive in anaerobic, waterlogged soils and convert nitrate to nitrogen gas, which escapes to the air. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so they are less active in waterlogged soil.

questions.stem: How does nitrogen in the proteins of a dead animal become available to plants again?
options: Denitrifying bacteria turn the proteins straight into nitrate for plants
Lightning breaks down the proteins into nitrogen gas, which plants absorb
Decomposers release ammonium, which nitrifying bacteria turn into nitrate
Plants absorb the animal's proteins directly through their root hairs
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down proteins and release ammonium (ammonification), and nitrifying bacteria convert it to nitrate for plant uptake. Plants cannot absorb whole proteins or use nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: A farmer grows a crop of lupins, a legume, and ploughs the plants into the soil before sowing wheat the next season. Why does the wheat grow better?
options: Lupins release oxygen into the soil, which wheat roots convert into nitrate
Nitrogen fixed by bacteria in lupin root nodules is released as the plants decompose
Lupins remove all nitrogen from the soil, so the wheat faces no competition for it
Lupins carry out denitrification, adding nitrate to the soil from the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Rhizobia in the lupin nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, and when the lupin residues decompose, ammonium and then nitrate become available to the wheat. Denitrification removes nitrate from soil rather than adding it.

questions.stem: What defines a keystone species?
options: It is the first species to colonise bare ground after a disturbance
Its effect on community structure is far greater than its abundance suggests
It is the most abundant species, and has the largest total biomass in the area
It is always a large predator at the top of every food chain in the area
questions.explanation: A keystone species plays a critical role in maintaining community structure, and its loss changes the ecosystem far more than its numbers or biomass would predict. Keystone species need not be predators.

questions.stem: When sea otters were hunted out of an area, sea urchins increased and kelp forests were heavily grazed, and many species that live in kelp declined. What does this show?
options: Sea urchins are a keystone species because their numbers increased
Kelp is a consumer that depends directly on sea otters for its food
The decline of species shows that otters competed with kelp for space
Sea otters are a keystone species whose loss changed the whole community
questions.explanation: Removing one predator triggered a chain of effects through the community, the mark of a keystone species. The urchins increased in response; their rise was the consequence, not the controlling role.

questions.stem: Why are keystone species often special targets for conservation?
options: They have no predators, so protecting them costs nothing at all
Protecting them helps maintain the structure of the whole community
They are always the rarest species, so they need the most protection
They are always endemic, so they are found in only one location
questions.explanation: Because many other species depend on the role a keystone species plays, conserving it helps protect the wider ecosystem. Scientists still debate whether single-species conservation is enough to maintain complex ecosystems.

questions.stem: Many eucalypts survive fire by sprouting new shoots from buds protected under thick bark. What are these buds called?
options: Root nodules
Stomata
Epicormic buds
Pneumatophores
questions.explanation: Epicormic buds lie dormant beneath the bark and sprout after fire damages the canopy. Some eucalypts also resprout from lignotubers at the base.

questions.stem: Many banksias hold their seeds in woody cones that open after fire. How does this benefit the species?
options: Seeds are released before fire, so that they burn and fertilise the soil
Seeds are kept inside the cones for good, so they are never eaten
Seeds open only in cool, wet weather, when fires never occur
Seeds are released onto cleared, nutrient-rich ground with less competition
questions.explanation: Fire triggers seed release onto an ash bed with more light and fewer competitors, giving seedlings a good start. This is one of many adaptations that make fire a dynamic factor in Australian ecosystems.

questions.stem: A heath contains a shrub that is killed by fire and regrows only from seed, taking 8 years to produce seed. What happens if fires occur every 4 years?
options: The shrub will increase, because frequent fire clears its competitors
The shrub is unaffected, because fire frequency does not change seeding
The shrub will start resprouting from buds to cope with the fires
The shrub may disappear, because plants burn before they can set seed
questions.explanation: If fire returns before the plants mature and set seed, the seed bank is not replenished and the species can be lost. Different fire regimes affect biodiversity differently, so fire frequency matters in management.

questions.stem: Which statement about fire in Australian ecosystems is correct?
options: Every fire reduces biodiversity, so all fires should always be prevented
Every fire increases biodiversity, so burning should be as often as possible
Fire affects only plants, because animals always escape the flames
The effect on biodiversity depends on fire frequency, intensity and season
questions.explanation: Some species need fire to regenerate while others are killed by it, so the fire regime determines which species persist. Too frequent, too intense or poorly timed fires can harm biodiversity.

questions.stem: A long drought reduces the growth of grasses in a reserve. What is the most likely effect on the carrying capacity for kangaroos?
options: It rises, because fewer plants means less competition for water
It falls, because less food is available to support the population
It rises, because the kangaroos have more space to spread out
It is unchanged, because carrying capacity depends only on predators
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the largest population the environment can support, and it depends on resources such as food and water. Climatic events such as drought can lower it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes ecological succession?
options: The cycling of nitrogen between the air, soil and organisms
The seasonal migration of animals between breeding areas
A series of changes in the species present in a habitat over time
The movement of energy from one trophic level to the next
questions.explanation: Succession is the gradual change in community composition as species colonise and modify a habitat. Energy flow and nutrient cycling are different ecosystem processes.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes primary from secondary succession?
options: Primary begins where soil remains; secondary begins on bare rock that has no soil
Primary involves only animals; secondary involves only plants and fungi
Primary is caused by humans; secondary happens only after volcanic eruptions
Primary begins on bare ground with no soil; secondary begins where soil remains
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts on newly exposed surfaces, such as lava flows or sand dunes, where soil must form. Secondary succession follows disturbances such as fire or clearing that leave soil and seeds behind, so it is usually faster.

questions.stem: Lichens are often the first organisms to grow on bare rock. How do they make it possible for other species to establish?
options: They break down rock and add organic matter, starting soil formation
They shade the rock so heavily that no other species can grow there
They release seeds that grow into the trees of the later community
They fix carbon into the rock, making it too hard for roots to enter
questions.explanation: Pioneer species such as lichens weather the rock and, as they die, add organic matter, building a thin soil that mosses and small plants can then colonise. Each stage changes abiotic conditions in ways that allow the next species to arrive.

questions.stem: During succession on a coastal dune, early plants increase soil depth, organic matter and shade. Which outcome is most likely?
options: No new species can arrive, because the soil is now too deep for roots
New species suited to the changed conditions replace some pioneer species
The pioneer species increase forever, because they made the conditions
The abiotic conditions return to the original bare sand within a year
questions.explanation: Changes in abiotic factors caused by the community favour other species, which can outcompete the pioneers, which in turn changes the conditions further. Succession is driven by this feedback between organisms and their environment.

questions.stem: Why is secondary succession after a bushfire usually faster than primary succession on a new lava flow?
options: Soil, seeds and roots remain after the fire, so plants re-establish quickly
Fire adds new rock to the area, which lichens colonise quickly
Lava flows contain more nutrients than soil, so growth is slower
Animals cannot return after fire, so plants face no grazing
questions.explanation: Secondary succession starts with soil, a seed bank and surviving roots and buds already in place. On fresh lava, soil must first be formed by pioneer species, which takes a long time.

questions.stem: Food webs and successional models are used to predict how an ecosystem will respond to change. What determines how reliable such a model is?
options: How representative the sample data used to build it are
How many colours and arrows are used to draw it
Whether it predicts that every species will survive
Whether it was built without any field data at all
questions.explanation: Models are built by interpreting and extrapolating from survey data, so their predictions are only as reliable as the sampling is representative. A model built on biased or too few samples may mislead managers.

questions.stem: A model of a wetland food web was built from quadrats placed only near the edge of the water. Why might its predictions be unreliable for the whole wetland?
options: Edge habitats always contain every species found in the wetland
The samples may not represent species and numbers across the whole wetland
Quadrats can never be used to collect data about plants in wetlands
Food web models cannot be built from any sampled data at all
questions.explanation: Sampling one zone may miss species or misjudge their abundance elsewhere, so extrapolating to the whole wetland introduces error. Random or stratified sampling across all zones would make the model more representative.

questions.stem: Why do ecologists use models to predict the impact of a proposed change, such as clearing part of a woodland?
options: To avoid having to collect any data from the woodland itself
To make the change happen more quickly once it is approved
To estimate likely effects on species before the change is made
To guarantee that no species will be affected by the change
questions.explanation: Models extrapolate from survey data to forecast how populations and interactions might respond, helping decision-makers weigh options. Their predictions carry uncertainty and depend on good data.
